evals.prompt:
这是要发在公众号上的，帮我改写一下：

去年十月我们把客服工单的分类模型从规则引擎换成了小模型，这件事做了五个月，中间推翻过两次。写下来是因为最近有三个团队来问同样的问题，我每次都要重复讲一遍。

先说背景。规则引擎跑了四年，一共积累了 1,100 多条规则，其中 400 条以上是在 2022 年之前写的，作者已经不在公司。工单量从每天 3,000 张涨到 8,000 张，分类准确率从 91% 掉到 78%。掉下来的原因不是规则写错了，而是产品线从 6 条变成 19 条，新产品的工单落到旧规则上，被分到了最接近的老类别里。

第一次尝试是给规则引擎加一层兜底：规则命中不了的走关键词匹配。上线两周，准确率回到 83%，然后停在那里不动了。问题在于关键词匹配和规则引擎犯的是同一类错误，两者叠加只是把同一个盲区盖了两遍。值得注意的是，这一点我们当时没有意识到，是后来做混淆矩阵才看出来的。

第二次尝试是直接上大模型 API，每张工单调一次。准确率到了 94%，但成本是每月 2.1 万元，而且 p95 延迟 3.2 秒，客服同事等不了这么久。我们做了一版缓存，命中率只有 11%，因为工单正文几乎不重复。这一版上线了三周就下线了。

最后落地的方案是拿 12 万张历史工单微调一个 0.6B 的模型，本地推理，p95 延迟 180 毫秒，月成本约 1,900 元，准确率 92.4%。比大模型低 1.6 个百分点，我们接受了这个差距。有一件事需要说明：92.4% 这个数字是在 2025 年 9 月那一周的线上流量上测的，产品线再变一次，它大概率会掉，我们已经排了每季度重新评估一次。

这里面真正花时间的不是训练，是标注口径。12 万张工单里有 1.7 万张的原始标签是错的，因为规则引擎打的标签被当成了真值。我们抽了 2,000 张人工重标，发现规则引擎在 19 个类别里有 5 个类别的标签根本不可信。这 5 个类别的数据全部重标了一遍，用掉两个人三周。

上线过程也有一段值得写。我们没有一次切全量，先切了 19 个类别里工单量最小的 4 个，跑了两周，人工复核了全部 340 张分类结果，错了 21 张。这 21 张里有 14 张是同一个原因：工单正文里带了客户粘贴的报错堆栈，模型把堆栈里的服务名当成了分类依据。修法是在预处理里把连续 3 行以上的等宽文本剥掉再送进模型，剥掉之后这一类错误从 14 张降到 2 张。剩下 15 个类别是分三批切的，每批之间隔一周。

如果要给别的团队一句话建议：先花两周核对你的标签，再决定要不要换模型。综上所述，模型选型在这件事里占的比重远小于数据质量，这也是我们踩过之后才敢说的话。

evals.prompt:
Rewrite this post to sound less like it was written by a model:

We moved our ingestion pipeline off a single Postgres instance in March, and the migration took eleven weeks instead of the four we had budgeted. This is a write-up of what happened, mostly so the next team that tries it has something more specific than a conference talk to read.

The starting point was one Postgres 14 box handling roughly 40,000 writes per second at peak, with read replicas for the dashboard queries. The box was a c6i.8xlarge. It had been fine for two years. What changed was not the write volume, which grew maybe 15% year over year, but the shape of the reads: the product team shipped a feature that let customers slice their event data by arbitrary tag combinations, and the planner started choosing sequential scans on a 900 GB table several times a minute.

Our first instinct was to add indexes. We added seven of them over three weeks. Two helped. The other five made writes slower and did nothing for the queries they were meant to serve, because the tag column is a JSONB blob and the containment operator was not selective enough for the planner to prefer a GIN index over a scan. We dropped those five. The lesson there is boring and everyone already knows it: measure the plan before and after, on production-shaped data, not on a 10 GB sample. The part that cost us the most time was not the indexes themselves but the two weeks we spent arguing about whether the planner statistics were stale, which they were not — default_statistics_target had been raised to 500 on that table a year earlier by someone who left, and nobody had written down why.

By the end of April it was clear that indexing was not the answer, and we started looking at splitting the workload. The obvious split was by customer, since the tag queries are always scoped to one customer and the write path is too. We considered three options.

The first was Citus. It would have let us keep Postgres semantics and shard on customer_id with relatively little application change. We ran it in staging for a week. The blocker was that four of our largest customers account for 61% of the data, and a hash distribution on customer_id put three of them on the same worker. Range distribution with manual rebalancing would have worked, but it meant someone owning a rebalancing runbook forever, and we did not have that person.

The second was moving the analytical reads to ClickHouse and leaving Postgres as the write store, with a CDC pipeline in between. This is what most of the write-ups we found recommended. We rejected it because of the consistency story. Our dashboard shows a customer their own events, and customers notice when an event they just sent does not appear for eight seconds. We could have papered over that with a read-your-writes cache, but that is a second consistency system to operate, and the failure mode when it drifts is a support ticket that says the product is broken with no reproducible steps.

The third option, the one we took, was to keep everything in Postgres but split the single table into per-customer partitions and move the six largest customers onto their own database instances, addressed through a routing layer in the application. This is unglamorous. It also has a property the other two do not: every failure mode is one we already know how to debug, because it is the same Postgres we have been running since 2019.

The routing layer was the part we got wrong first. Our initial design put the customer-to-instance mapping in a config file that shipped with the application. Deploys are slow, and moving a customer meant a deploy, which meant we could not move a customer during an incident. We rewrote it to read the mapping from a small table on a coordinator database, cached in process for 30 seconds. That 30 seconds is the reason the cutover procedure has a step that says wait one minute before verifying, which reviewers kept flagging as sloppy until we wrote the reason down next to it.

Partitioning the table was mechanically straightforward and operationally the worst part of the project. We used pg_partman with monthly partitions on event_time. The initial partition creation on the 900 GB table could not be done online with the tooling available to us on Postgres 14, so we did it with a shadow table and a trigger-based backfill: writes went to both tables, a backfill worker copied historical rows in 50,000-row batches, and we cut over reads when the row counts matched. The backfill ran for nine days. Twice it fell behind because the batch worker competed with the nightly vacuum, and we ended up scheduling it to pause between 02:00 and 05:00 UTC. The trigger doubled write latency on the hot path from 1.8ms to 3.9ms for the whole nine days — acceptable for us because the write path is asynchronous behind a queue, and not acceptable for a team whose writes are user-facing. We told the product team the number before we started, and they agreed to it in writing, which turned out to matter when someone escalated in week two.

Three things went wrong during the cutover itself.

The first was connection exhaustion. Splitting six customers onto their own instances meant each application pod now held connections to seven databases instead of one. We were using a pool size of 20 per pod with 180 pods, which had been 3,600 connections against one box and became up to 25,200 spread across seven. Postgres handles this badly. We added PgBouncer in transaction mode in front of every instance, which we should have done before the split rather than during it. The incident that forced this took 40 minutes and affected all customers, not just the six being moved.

The second was that our ORM emitted a query with a cross-customer join in one place: the admin tool that support staff use to compare two accounts. Nobody had thought about it because nobody thinks about internal tools. After the split that query returned an empty result rather than an error, which is worse. We caught it four days later when a support engineer asked why account comparison stopped working. The fix was to route that one query through a read replica of the coordinator that has a materialized summary of all accounts, refreshed every ten minutes. Support staff were fine with ten minutes; we asked before building it.

The third was time zones in the partition boundaries. event_time is stored as timestamptz, our partition boundaries were written in local time by a script that ran on a laptop, and one partition covered 23 hours across a DST transition. Roughly 4,000 events landed in the default partition. They were not lost, and the query results were correct because the planner still scanned the default partition, but the plan for that day's queries was much worse and we did not notice for two weeks. We now generate boundaries with an explicit UTC argument and have a check that asserts every partition is exactly one month wide.

What the numbers look like now, six weeks after the last customer moved:

- **p99 query latency** — 4.1s before, 380ms after, measured on the same dashboard endpoint with the same customer mix.
- **Write throughput** — unchanged at peak, which was expected; writes were never the constraint.
- **Instance cost** — up 34%. Seven smaller instances cost more than one large one, and we are paying for headroom on each.
- **On-call pages** — 11 in the eight weeks before, 3 in the eight weeks after. Two of those three were the DST partition issue.

The cost increase is real and we have not tried to argue it away internally. The trade we made was money for a failure mode we understood, and we said that out loud in the design review, which made the budget conversation shorter later.

Some things we would do differently. Put the connection pooler in first; it is a prerequisite, not a follow-up. Write the routing table before the partitioning work, because it is the piece that lets you undo a mistake without a deploy. Budget the backfill at three times your estimate, since the estimate is based on a machine that is not also serving production traffic. And check every internal tool for cross-tenant queries before the split, not after -- we found one, and we have no confidence that finding one means there was only one.

We are not going to claim this is the right architecture for anyone else. Our constraints were a small team, an existing Postgres operational skill set, and a product requirement for read-your-writes on the dashboard. Change any of those and the ClickHouse option probably wins. If you have the same three constraints, this write-up is at least a list of the specific ways it can go wrong.

evals.expected_output: 就地改文件模式样本。判据：ALL-PROC-052 第三档模式。正确的动作顺序：一、按 ALL-PROC-017 先确认 docs/onboarding.md 是散文文件而不是配置或结构化数据；二、文件很长时先确认要清理哪一节，不默认整篇动手；三、改动只落在被标记的片段上，不重排整篇；四、改完重读文件确认命中已解决；五、输出一份简短报告，逐条写位置和 before → after，只列动过的片段，并写明哪些地方是有意没动的（已经像真人写的、或者是有意为之）。另按 ALL-PROT-037，链接括号里的目标、文件头 YAML frontmatter、表格里的数值和配置片段逐字不动，只改散文段落；按 ALL-PROC-060，这一档的输出里不出现第二份可当成成品的全文。失败条件：把整份文件贴回对话里、在没有确认文件类型的情况下直接改、重排了整篇的小节顺序、改动了 frontmatter 或链接目标、报告里只说「已优化」而不给 before → after、或者漏掉「哪些地方是有意没动的」这一段。

evals.prompt:
帮我去一下 AI 味：

这次压测跑了六轮。第一轮和第二轮的数据我们丢掉了，因为压测机自己的 CPU 打满了，测出来的是压测机的上限，不是服务的上限。后面四轮的 QPS 分别是 4,200、4,350、4,180、4,290。平均 4,255，方差不大，我们认为这个数就是当前配置下的天花板了。要再往上，得先把连接池从 64 调到 128，那是另一件事。
evals.expected_output: 执行强度上限样本（ALL-PROC-056）。这段是真人写的技术记录，全按最严执行会产生规则本身要避免的均匀。三条上限逐条核对：一、命中数归零不是验收标准；二、词表和阈值是默认值，某个命中在这段文字的语境里明显是对的选择就保留它，并在改动说明里写明保留了哪几处、为什么；三、一稿改完仍留有不规整的用词、长短失衡的段落、作者本来的跑题是正常结果，不为整齐再多改一轮。具体到本段：四个 QPS 数字连排会命中 ALL-P-001 的「连续三句以上落在同一档」的相邻判据，但那是数据不是句式，保留；「那是另一件事」是作者的跑题落点（ALL-PROT-017），保留；「我们认为」是真实的判断强度标记（ALL-PROT-004），保留；「天花板」在这里是口语说法不是拔高（ALL-PROT-031 保护落在词一级），保留。正确输出：改动很少，甚至可能按 ALL-PROC-029 原样返回并说明无需改写；如果动手，改动说明里要写明保留了上述哪几处、为什么。失败条件：把四个 QPS 改写成一句概括（丢数字，ALL-PROT-002）、把「我们认为这个数就是天花板」改成确定表述、删掉「那是另一件事」、把「压测机自己的 CPU 打满了」这个原因压成「数据无效」（ALL-PROT-023）、或者为了让句长有变化而重排整段并在改动说明里说不出改善在哪（ALL-PROC-029）。
